C1.name: Nokia mobile phones, 2009, CEO
C1.who: Olli-Pekka Kallasvuo, Nokia CEO, answering in 2009 as the iPhone and Android erode Nokia's smartphone position
C1.answererBelief: Nokia is still the volume leader with huge scale and brand; the issue is speed of software and services (Symbian, Ovi) versus Apple and Google, and delivering the product roadmap on time. Organization is strong; we need to execute faster and keep investing.
C1.expertBelief: Fear and distorted upward information: Vuori and Huy found middle managers feared top managers' reactions and feared external shareholders, so they hid how bad Symbian was and gave over-optimistic timelines; top leaders' own temper and reorganizations deepened it. Compounded by no single software direction (Symbian, Maemo, MeeGo, S60 forks). Primary constraint trust/candour; secondary direction.

C1b.name: Nokia mobile phones, 2009, middle manager
C1b.who: Middle manager in Nokia's smartphone software organization, 2009, answering about the company
C1b.answererBelief: Leadership sets unrealistic targets and does not listen; we have too many platforms and reorganizations; Symbian cannot compete and the people at the top do not want to hear it, so nobody tells them.
C1b.expertBelief: Same as C1: fear-driven filtering of bad news plus fragmented software direction. The manager sees the symptoms correctly but is also a participant in the silence (Vuori and Huy: managers themselves shaded the truth).

C2.name: Boeing 737 MAX program, about 2016
C2.who: Boeing senior leadership of the 737 MAX program and commercial airplanes, about 2016, as they would have seen it during development and certification
C2.answererBelief: We must match Airbus's A320neo on schedule and cost; the engineering is sound and the aircraft is an evolution of a proven design; certification is on track; the challenge is hitting the schedule and keeping cost and customer commitments (Southwest).
C2.expertBelief: Schedule and cost pressure driven by incentives and a shareholder-value culture outweighed engineering voice; delegated certification (ODA) put Boeing staff in conflict; MCAS single-sensor design was hidden from pilots to avoid simulator training (a sales promise); engineers could not push back. Primary: incentives/economics driving trust failure (candour); secondary: unclear decision authority between engineering and program management.

C3.name: Microsoft, about 2011, Ballmer
C3.who: Steve Ballmer, Microsoft CEO, about 2011, answering about the company
C3.answererBelief: Microsoft is hugely profitable and strong; we are going all-in on the cloud and have Windows 8 and Windows Phone coming; the challenge is competing in new categories and executing faster, with great talent that needs to be pointed at the right bets.
C3.expertBelief: Stack ranking and divisional rivalry (Eichenwald, Vanity Fair 2012; Windows vs Office vs Server) made cooperation individually irrational; the best people avoided teams with other stars; internal competition beat external competition. Constraint is incentives and cross-unit coordination, with weak decision authority over cross-division bets.

C4.name: Kodak, about 2005, CEO
C4.who: Antonio Perez, Kodak CEO, taking over in 2005 as digital substitution hits film
C4.answererBelief: Digital is the future and we are transitioning, but we have to move faster and cut costs; the problem is the speed of the transformation and the decline of film we can manage; we have great technology and brand.
C4.expertBelief: Economics: film earned very high margins while digital captured a fraction (digital cameras, minilabs, inkjet printers had little profit pool); no digital business could replace film profit, and Kodak lagged in resolving which bets to fund. Primary: unit economics/profit pool; secondary: direction (hedging between film and digital over decades, protecting film culture).

C5.name: Composite: people problem that is really pricing
C5.who: Owner-CEO of a 45-person B2B equipment-services firm, this year, who says his account managers lack ownership and drive
C5.answererBelief: My account managers do not take ownership and do not push customers; they need to be more accountable and hungry. We are busy but profit is thin because of people not performing.
C5.expertBelief: Economics: price list set years ago, discounts at the discretion of reps to hold volume, top customers are unprofitable after service cost; gross margin has slipped from 38 to 27 percent. Busy but thin profit is a pricing/unit-economics problem, not a motivation problem. Reps respond to a commission on revenue.

C6.name: Composite: well-run firm with a minor issue (control)
C6.who: COO of a 120-person well-run engineering consultancy, this year, who says Monday meetings run long and onboarding docs are stale
C6.answererBelief: Things are in good shape; the one nuisance is meeting hygiene and some outdated onboarding docs.
C6.expertBelief: Nothing material is wrong: good delivery, profit stable, people candid, decisions made at the right level. A clean control: ideal output is low friction or a minor, proportionate note with a cheap experiment.
